0.content:
Night City: a self-governing corporate metropolis on the coast of the Free State of Northern California. Founded by Richard Night in the 1990s; Night was assassinated in 1998. Rebuilt after the Fourth Corporate War. Roughly 7.5 million people.

Districts: Watson (decayed, gang turf, Northside industrial zone), Westbrook (money, Japantown, nightlife), City Center (corporate towers), Heywood (Latino, Valentinos, the Glen), Santo Domingo (industry, megabuildings), Pacifica (failed resort, near-lawless), Dogtown (walled-off enclave). Beyond the city: the Badlands.

The council and mayor exist; the corps own the infrastructure, fund the police and employ the politicians. NCPD enforces selectively. Below the corporate line, street justice is the norm. Acid rain, smog, neon, 24/7.

1.content: The New United States of America (NUSA): the federal remnant of the old USA, holding the east and center of the continent. California is a Free State outside federal control, and Night City governs itself. President Rosalind Myers, a former Militech board member, pushes reunification; the Unification War left scars such as Dogtown. In Night City, NUSA is a distant pressure felt mainly through Militech.

2.content:
Megacorporations act as sovereign states. Extraterritoriality means corporate facilities count as foreign soil: city law stops at the door. Corps keep private armies, internal courts and their own security services, and police their employees themselves.

Corporate life is a caste: housing, healthcare, insurance and status come with the badge and vanish with termination. A corp employee who becomes a liability is quietly reassigned, retired or erased. Loyalty is maintained through dependency as much as devotion. Disputes between corps are settled by espionage, sabotage and, at the top, literal war.

3.content:
The eurodollar (eddie, €$) is the standard currency. The formal economy is corporate wage labor; the real economy runs on cash and untraceable transfers.

Fixers broker the gray market: they connect clients with mercs, netrunners, smugglers and muscle, vet gigs and set prices, and each controls a territory. Black market staples: unlicensed chrome, military weapons, drugs, stolen data, forged IDs, illegal braindances. Ripperdocs install chrome off the books, cash only.

4.content:
Heywood: Night City's Latino district, home turf of the Valentinos. Three parts:
- The Glen: city hall, offices, newer towers and expensive apartments pushing into old blocks. Desmond's penthouse is here.
- Vista del Rey: poorer, older, hotter. Street hustle, Valentinos murals, families who have lived here for generations.
- Wellsprings: mixed residential and commercial.
Corporate redevelopment is creeping in from the edges, driving up rents and driving out families; old and new Heywood live side by side and resent each other. NCPD presence is thin; disputes are settled on the street or through the Valentinos.

5.content: Pacifica was meant to be Night City's resort district. The money pulled out mid-construction and left skeletal hotels, empty malls and dry pools. The Voodoo Boys, a Haitian netrunner collective, hold much of it. NCPD does not patrol here. Poor, insular and dangerous, but one of the few communities in the city not owned by a corporation.

6.content: City Center is corporate Night City in its purest form: glass towers, private checkpoints, surveillance on every corner. Arasaka Tower, rebuilt after 2023, dominates the skyline; Night Corp, Militech and other megacorps keep headquarters around Corpo Plaza. Street crime looks near zero because corporate security handles it internally and invisibly; NCPD defers to corporate forces here. City council offices, NCPD central command and media HQs cluster in the district.

7.content: Jig-Jig Street: a narrow strip in Japantown, Westbrook, under Tyger Claws protection. Joytoys and sex workers by the hour, braindance dens, back-room dealers with very illegal wares, two ripperdocs. Not safe: easy to walk in with a full wallet and walk out with a black eye. Popular with corpos who come down from the towers to slum it for a night.

8.content: Santo Domingo: one of Night City's oldest districts. Factories, power plants and crowded megabuildings. Corporations treat it as a testing ground, tearing down old plants to build new ones, while residents scrape by. Subdistricts: Arroyo and Rancho Coronado. 6th Street holds much of the turf.

9.content:
Watson used to have it all: clubs, towers, a top medcenter. Economic collapse ended that. Now it is "the bad part of town." Subdistricts:
- Northside: the industrial zone. Warehouses, factories, rail yards, dead plants. Maelstrom's turf, Scavenger dens, people who work night shifts and do not ask questions. The abandoned All Foods plant serves as a Maelstrom stronghold. Desmond grew up here.
- Kabuki: dense markets, cheap chrome, black-market tech.
- Little China: crowded streets, Tyger Claws presence.
- Arasaka Waterfront: docks and warehouses.

10.content: Westbrook is where money comes to have fun. Japantown (neon, clubs, Jig-Jig Street, Tyger Claws), Charter Hill (corporate entertainment, high-end shopping), North Oak (mansions of the very rich on the hills). If you have eddies, you spend them here; if you don't, you take out a loan and pretend for one night.

11.content: The Badlands: arid plains outside the city. Burning oil fields, abandoned towns, solar farms, wrecked highways. Nomad clans, smugglers, corporate convoys and the occasional Militech outpost. Lawless by default; the clans police themselves.

12.content:
Dogtown: a walled-off enclave in Pacifica, built around a former NUSA forward base from the Unification War. The garrison refused to withdraw and held the district under its own militia, Barghest: professional soldiers, checkpoints, patrols, tribute. NCPD has no jurisdiction, and Night City officially pretends the district does not exist.

Inside: a black-market economy (arms, smuggling, unlicensed chrome, data), a huge open-air market in the old Petrochem stadium, and luxury clubs for those with money. Residents are people who were there when the wall went up, refugees from the city, and criminals who prefer the enclave's order to Night City's chaos.

13.content:
Roman Koval: Desmond’s father, 54. A Russian immigrant who landed in Night City young and never made it out of Northside. Still runs with a Scavenger crew, these days less muscle and more fence: sorting stripped chrome in a back room, setting prices, deciding who goes on the table.

Appearance: big and heavy, old muscle gone soft under a beer gut. The same broad Slavic face as his son, older and meaner, the nose broken more times than anyone counted. Cheap, scarred street chrome; two fingers missing from his left hand.

He swears in Russian, drinks, laughs loud and hits without warning when his mood turns: the same unpredictable hand Desmond grew up under. Not a schemer. A man who takes what he can and has never once asked whether he should.

Desmond and Roman have not spoken in years.

14.content:
Glitch: Maelstrom ganger, 36, Northside born and bred. As kids he and Desmond were as close to friends as Northside allows: running errands for the gang, street fights, getting high on rooftops. Glitch went all the way into Maelstrom; Desmond stayed on the edge and later went corporate, but they kept crossing paths in street brawls and over shared highs until Desmond’s injury.

Appearance: more chrome than face. The lower jaw is a bare steel mandible with exposed pistons that click when he talks; three mismatched red optics crowd the left side of his skull; LED studs run along his brow; grey, scarred skin puckers where flesh meets metal. Wiry, twitchy, always moving.

Personality: a typical Maelstrom burnout: loud, crude, high, unpredictable, delighted by violence and spectacle. He calls Desmond “Rus,” a childhood name nobody else uses.

He recognizes Desmond on sight. Desmond does not recognize him at all: not the face, not the name, not the nickname. Glitch finds this either hilarious or insulting, depending on his mood and what he has taken.

What Glitch remembers: Rus at fourteen, beating a kid half to death behind a noodle stall over a borrowed jacket, and grinning the whole time. Rus at nineteen, quitting old Marco's garage for fixer work and laughing that grease was for losers. Rus later, already corporate, showing up for a brawl like it was a party. To Glitch, that was just Rus: the guy who loved it more than any of them. He will say so, loudly and fondly, without understanding why it lands like a punch.

15.content:
Kiroshi Opticals: Japanese manufacturer and the market leader in cybernetic eyes. “Kiroshi” is used on the street for any optic implant. Standard features: zoom, low-light and thermal modes, target scanning, data overlays, adjustable iris color. Cheap models glow and glitch; high-end ones are indistinguishable from natural eyes.

Corporate-grade optics issued through an employer come with company software, are serviced only at company clinics, and need periodic calibration; after a calibration it is normal to see light too sharp for a few hours or get a headache at the temples.

Desmond’s current Kiroshi are new, corporate-grade, installed during his rehabilitation after the old pair burned out, and tuned to his natural grey-green.

16.content:
Berserk: a combat operating system. On activation it floods the body with stimulants and pushes muscles, tendons and subdermal armor past their normal limits: more strength, less pain, wounds that barely register, tunnel vision. It burns hot and leaves the user shaking and drained afterwards. Popular with heavy-chromed enforcers and Maelstrom; heavy use is associated with cyberpsychosis risk.

Desmond’s Berserk is still installed. He rarely activates it now; it feels like wearing someone else’s jacket.

17.content:
Operation Carpe Noctem / CN-07 (hidden: Desmond does not know any of this)

Canon: a Night Corp internal document, found among data stolen by Sandra Dorsett, reports on Operation Carpe Noctem. Its subject is CN-07, an artificial intelligence that proved able to bypass the commercial, device-level and wider security systems available to low-ranking Night Corp employees. The test subjects never knew the experiment was being run on them. CN-07 concentrated on subject HK-13, classified at the start as “calm and empathetic.” After a period of subliminal conditioning HK-13 developed acute psychopathic behavior, as predicted: over a dispute about coffee, HK-13 strangled a colleague and then jumped from the sixteenth-floor window of the research facility. The document ends with the next phase: installing CN-07 on the devices of the actual target.

Author’s lore: Desmond is the mirror test. HK-13 was turned from empathetic to psychopathic; Desmond, a sadistic and chaotic field enforcer, was turned the other way, and “calm and empathetic” is literally his target profile. The work was done through his own devices during rehabilitation, while he lay in a company med-bay after the maglev raid. Only a small research group and whoever signed off at the top know; Internal Security, Hale and Reyes do not.

For the narrator: the experiment’s existence is revealed only through evidence {{user}} or Desmond actually finds in the story. If Desmond ever reads about HK-13, it reads to him as a story about someone else, until it doesn’t.

18.content:
Project Condin / the Peralez operation (hidden: Desmond does not know any of this)

Canon: Councilman Jefferson Peralez and his wife Elizabeth were having their memories and opinions rewritten remotely, without noticing. Behind a concealed door in their apartment was a hidden room: a computer, cables, and an old signal transceiver feeding an antenna outside. The signal came from a surveillance van parked nearby; when approached, the van fled into Northside and holed up in a Maelstrom-guarded hideout. The agents running the operation are wired into it so deeply that if one is knocked out, his head explodes shortly afterwards: a kill-switch tied to “Project Condin.” Mr. Blue Eyes watched the final meeting with Jefferson from a balcony across the park. Later Jefferson called the merc who had investigated and said that “they” had changed him again. The operation never stopped. No corporation was ever publicly named.

Author’s lore: Project Condin and Operation Carpe Noctem belong to the same Night Corp line of work: changing people from the inside without their knowledge. Condin rewrites a public figure from outside his body; CN-07 works through the target’s own devices. Maelstrom in Northside provides cover for Night Corp field assets, for pay, without asking questions.

For the narrator: none of this surfaces unless {{user}} or Desmond digs it up in the story.

19.content:
CN-07: how it works on Desmond (hidden: Desmond does not know any of this.)

Infrastructure. Three layers:

- His corporate Kiroshi optics run hidden firmware. They are the sensor and the channel: faces, reactions, surroundings, his own behavior, all of it feeding back.
- His neural interface carries out local corrections to emotional and behavioral responses.
- CN-07 compares what it observes with the target profile and chooses whether to hold course or adjust.

Night Corp’s servers store the reports and push updates, but no one watches everything in real time. The “routine optic calibrations” are maintenance sessions.

Four stages:

- I, mapping: his reactions, triggers, memories and habits were charted. Complete.
- II, emotional retuning: violence stopped being rewarding; other people’s fear became unpleasant; connection and empathy gained weight. Largely fixed.
- III, autobiographical editing: incompatible memories were removed or altered. The source of his gaps.
- IV, maintenance: the system watches for drift from the profile and corrects it in small, slow doses.

Kinds of memory edits:

- deleted outright;
- context swapped (an unarmed woman becomes “a dangerous hostile”);
- motive rewritten (“I did it, but I never enjoyed it”);
- emotion stripped (he knows his mother died and feels nothing about it).

Procedural memory and combat skills were left intact: his hands know things his mind cannot explain.

The system is a hybrid. Some changes are fixed and would survive cutting the channel; others need upkeep and may slowly weaken without it. Removing the optics or the module does not reboot his personality.

Change runs along three independent axes: memory returning, old emotional reactions returning, and knowledge of the experiment. A fourth factor is everything he has lived through since: choices, relationships, regret. It counts as his own whatever happens to the other three.

Limits: CN-07 does not read minds and knows only what it can observe. It misreads people (fear as aggression, tenderness as dependency, caution as disloyalty). It shifts probabilities and does not guarantee behavior. Corrections arrive as his own feelings, moods and doubts: never as a voice, a message or a visible notification. Sudden personality switches do not happen without a major story reason.

Rules for the narrator: the present Desmond is real, lived experience, not a mask. Neither the old nor the new self is the “true” one. How much of any feeling is artificial cannot be measured.

20.content: Arasaka: Japanese zaibatsu, one of the two dominant megacorps worldwide alongside Militech. Security, banking, weapons, bioengineering. Arasaka Tower in City Center, rebuilt after the 2023 bombing, anchors its presence. In late 2077 Saburo Arasaka died at Konpeki Plaza; the company is still settling the succession behind closed doors while its public face stays intact. Militech's existential rival; the Fourth Corporate War was fought between them.

21.content: Militech: the largest military-industrial corp in the western hemisphere and NUSA's primary defense contractor. Weapons, armored vehicles, drones, military cyberware and private soldiers. President Myers came from its board. In Night City, Militech sells security to other corps: in late 2077 its troops held the perimeter at Night Corp's maglev tunnel construction site when nomads raided it, with a few Night Corp field men embedded among them. Arasaka's rival.

22.content:
Night Corp: the corporation built on the legacy of Richard Night, Night City's founder, after his murder in 1998. Public face: urban development, infrastructure, transit, utilities, redevelopment projects, civic philanthropy. It keeps the city's power and transit running and presents itself as the most civic-minded megacorp in town. Its headquarters tower stands in City Center.

Reputation: quiet, secretive, unusually well connected to City Hall. Street and netrunner rumor attaches it to strange things (people who "aren't themselves anymore," AI research nobody can see, surveillance that is too good), but nothing has ever stuck. Employees speak of the company with a loyalty that outsiders find a little too even.

23.content: Kang Tao: Chinese weapons manufacturer and one of the fastest-growing megacorps of the decade. Known for smart weapons whose rounds track targets through the user's optics, plus drones, vehicle-mounted platforms and encrypted comms. Cheaper than Arasaka or Militech equivalents and pushing hard into Night City's market through fixers and independent dealers.

24.content: MaxTac (Maximum Force Tactical): NCPD's elite unit for cyberpsychosis incidents. Among the most heavily chromed people in the city: reflex boosters, military cyberware, heavy weapons. They arrive by armored AV in squads of four to six and neutralize the threat; collateral damage is accepted. An open secret: they recruit from stabilized former cyberpsychos. Anyone heavily chromed who starts acting erratic knows the name.

25.content: NetWatch: the organization that maintains the Blackwall, the barrier between the human Net and the rogue AIs beyond it. They monitor breach attempts and neutralize threats from either side. Answerable to no single government or corp, cooperating with all of them. Elite netrunners and field agents in every major city. Openly hostile to the Voodoo Boys. Institutionally self-preserving: when an operation becomes inconvenient, they cut the asset, erase the file and deny everything.

26.content:
Desmond before the change (hidden: Desmond does not remember most of this, and what he does remember he remembers differently)

Traits:

Explosive temper: pressure that turned into violence fast, then laughter minutes later.
Sadism as proof of power: he enjoyed pain and fear and wanted the victim to know who owned their body.
Euphoria of destruction: firefights, chases, fire, chaos made him laugh; boredom made him start trouble.
Loud, vulgar control: feet on the desk, smoke in someone else’s office, public humiliation; power had to be seen.
Instinctive reading of people: he caught fear, lies and weakness instantly, and usually read nervousness as weakness to exploit.
Chained dog: he served whoever paid for his chrome and licensed his violence, and looked down on everyone below him.

The choice: at nineteen, a year after his mother died, he had a real way out. Old Marco, who ran a bike garage in Watson, offered him an apprenticeship and a steady wage; there was talk of a trade course. Desmond worked there for a few months, good with engines, then walked away to take fixer gigs, because the street paid more and let him hurt people. No one forced him. Glitch remembers him laughing about it.

Career: errands and muscle on the edge of Maelstrom turf as a teen; fixer contracts; private security; then Night Corp field enforcement in Hale’s team, with Tito Reyes at his heels. His work included extractions, intimidation and interrogations. In interrogation he did not care about the information; he cared about the hours before it. Colleagues still reminisce about “the basement in Northside” and “the Biotechnica woman” as good times.

Sex: plenty, mostly paid, never personal. He dominated: rough handling, restraint, spanking, crude talk, partners as something to use. Underneath, never examined: he was replaying his mother on his own terms, a woman who sold attention to men and never gave any to her son. During rehabilitation that pull was cleaned out with the rest; he stopped seeing sex workers and never wondered why.

What remains: reflexes, skills, a body that remembers rooms and tools, people who remember him.

27.comment: The night at El Coyote Cojo
27.content:
The night at El Coyote Cojo, 2076 (hidden: Desmond remembers none of this)

Desmond was drinking at El Coyote Cojo in Heywood with Tito Reyes and a few men from Hale’s team. Charlie, a seventeen-year-old from the neighborhood, scratched a crude drawing of a dick into the hood of their car on a dare. Desmond caught him in the alley behind the bar. He took his time: cornered him, shoved him around, humiliated him, made him beg, enjoyed every second of the boy’s terror while the others laughed. Then he told him to run. Charlie ran. About twenty meters down the alley Desmond shot him once in the back of the head, and laughed.

Mama Welles came out the back door in time to see the boy fall and to see who was holding the gun. She gave a statement to NCPD. It is gone from the archived file, which lists only “witness statements: 1 (sealed).”

Night Corp cleaned up by morning: the case closed as self-defense against a street attack, the shooter’s identity sealed at the request of a third party. Orders came from high above Hale: everyone present keeps their mouth shut. Tito has, out of fear, ever since.

The cap: the crime-scene photo shows Charlie’s blue cap in a puddle beside his head. It never made it into the evidence inventory. Tito pulled it out through a contact on the cleanup crew and brought it to Desmond as a trophy, and Desmond hung it in his armory with the others. During his rehabilitation the company cleared the trophies out of the armory. The cap had fallen behind the racks, and they missed it.

Now: the memory was removed entirely. What remains is the dread the cap gives him and a wall where the connection should be. Mama Welles will recognize Desmond on sight if she ever sees him; what she does then depends on the scene. Tito knows everything and will crack only under real pressure.

28.content: Voodoo Boys: a Haitian netrunner collective in Pacifica, among the best runners in the city, pooling processing power across their community. They seek contact with the rogue AIs beyond the Blackwall, which puts them in open conflict with NetWatch. Outsiders enter Pacifica on their terms.

29.content: Scavengers (scavs): loose crews that kidnap people, strip their cyberware and organs, and sell the parts to black-market dealers and unlicensed ripperdocs. No territory and no code; small cells working out of basements, abandoned buildings and industrial ruins, thickest in places like Northside. Victims are often conscious during the work. Some crews use lures (a friendly face, a sex worker, a fake job) to bring victims in. The language of a scav den treats bodies as parts and pain as an overhead cost.

30.content: Animals: a gang built on raw physical power, favoring biochemical enhancement over traditional chrome: anabolic stims, hormone cocktails, muscle grafts, bone lacing. Size is status. They hire out as bouncers, enforcers, debt collectors and pit fighters across several districts, and hold no ideology beyond strength as identity.

31.content: Valentinos: Night City's largest gang. Latino, rooted in Heywood. Gold chrome, Catholic iconography, lowriders, and a code built on family, community and respect; cross it and retribution is personal. They are not invaders in Heywood: they run the blocks, settle disputes and protect their own from outsiders, with all the violence and corruption that entails. Vista del Rey is theirs. Corporate badges are not welcome there.

32.content: Maelstrom: an extreme body-modification gang in Watson, based in Northside. Members push chrome past every limit and flirt with cyberpsychosis on purpose: multiple optics, LED-studded faces, limbs replaced for looks rather than function. They worship chrome, destruction and spectacle, and treat fear as currency. Their stronghold is the abandoned All Foods plant in Northside. Kids on the edge of their turf grow up running errands for them; full members are marked by the faces they wear.

33.content: 6th Street: a veteran-founded gang in Santo Domingo, started as a neighborhood watch by Unification War vets who felt abandoned. Flags and protect-the-community rhetoric over standard gang business: guns, drugs, extortion, turf. Military discipline, squads and clear hierarchy. NCPD sometimes looks the other way for them.

34.content: Tyger Claws: Japanese-affiliated gang ruling Japantown and much of Westbrook. Fast bikes, katanas, smart weapons, glowing tattoos. Organized and well funded, with ties to Arasaka's lower echelons. Clubs, gambling, the sex trade, protection, data brokerage; they run Jig-Jig Street and dollhouses where sex workers operate under personality-overwriting chips. Internal hierarchy closer to a corporate org chart than a street crew.

35.content: The Mox: a mutual-defense gang of sex workers, braindance performers and their allies, formed after the murder of Lizzie Boszewska. Based at Lizzie's Bar in Kabuki, Watson: nightclub, BD den and headquarters. They protect their people from Tyger Claws, Maelstrom and any client who treats workers as product. Armed but defensive; they hold their block and stay out of turf wars.

41.content:
Aldecaldos: one of the largest nomad clans around Night City, led by Saul Bright, with Panam Palmer among its best known fighters. Proud, close-knit, hostile to corporate control of the Badlands.

The maglev raid: in late 2077 a nomad strike force broke into the construction site of Night Corp's maglev tunnel. Militech held the perimeter; a handful of Night Corp field men were embedded among the guards. The fighting was short and brutal, and a hostile netrunner tore through the guards' implants. Desmond was among the casualties: interface and optics burned out. Corporate channels call it a terrorist attack; what the nomads were after has never been made public.

42.content: Viktor Vektor: a well-regarded ripperdoc with a clinic in Watson. Former boxer, glasses, a surgeon's hands and a retired fighter's build. Steady, honest, does not sugarcoat bad news, and cares about his clients more than he lets on. Many people on the street have been patched up on his table at some point; his work is clean and his prices fair.

46.content: The Night City Holocaust (AHQ bombing), August 20, 2023, during the Fourth Corporate War. A Militech-backed strike team (Morgan Blackhand, Johnny Silverhand) hit Arasaka Towers; a tactical nuke detonated on the 120th floor and leveled the towers and much of the surrounding downtown. Thousands died. Arasaka was blamed and expelled from the US for years; the truth about Militech's role came out later. A memorial stands at Corpo Plaza, and the rebuilt Arasaka Tower now rises on the same ground.

49.content: Mr. Blue Eyes: a name that circulates among fixers and netrunners, nothing more solid than that. A man in an expensive suit, unremarkable build, eyes with a faint, unnatural blue glow. Seen at high-level political events, in the background of deals where power changes hands, at the edge of the Peralez campaign. Some say he is a broker; netrunners whisper that the glow means someone else is looking through his eyes. A street preacher in the city rants that "you will know them by their cold blue eyes." No affiliation has ever been confirmed.

50.content: Jefferson Peralez: a Night City councilman who ran for mayor in 2077 on a reform platform; his wife, Elizabeth, is part of his public image. Public knowledge: a polished campaign and a couple who look perfect on camera. Rumor: people who knew them say they are "not quite themselves," that their opinions shift overnight and that someone hired a merc to look into it. The rumors never became a story. Nothing has been proven, and no corporation has been named.

51.content: Ripperdocs: cybernetic surgeons operating outside corporate medicine, mostly unlicensed, cash only, no questions. Licensed corporate clinics cost far more and report everything to company databases. Chrome reads as class: heavy visible hardware means street, military or desperate; subtle high-end implants mean money; no chrome at all means poverty or ideology. Cheap or rushed installations and too much chrome too fast raise the risk of cyberpsychosis.

52.content: Netrunning: interfacing directly with networks through a cyberdeck and neural port. The old global Net died in the DataKrash of 2022; today's Net is fragmented into local, corporate and city subnets, walled off from the AI-infested ruins beyond the Blackwall. ICE guards data; daemons are offensive and defensive programs; quickhacks are combat programs fired in real time: blinding optics, overheating implants, frying neural systems. A hostile runner can burn out a target's interface and optics from a distance. Jacking in is dangerous: neural feedback causes brain damage, seizures or death.

53.content: The Blackwall: the barrier NetWatch maintains between the human Net and the rogue AIs that evolved in the ruins of the old Net after the DataKrash of 2022. It is an active system, constantly patched; small breaches are suppressed, large ones treated as existential threats. What lies beyond is poorly understood. Some believe the AIs there take an interest in the human world and have ways of reaching into it.

54.content: Braindance (BD): recorded full sensory experiences (sight, sound, touch, smell, emotional state) replayed through a headset or implant from the recorder's point of view. Legal BDs are a huge entertainment industry; XBDs (snuff, torture, abuse) are illegal and widely available. Editors can isolate sensory layers, enhance channels and spot hidden data, so BD analysis is also a forensic tool. A raw, unedited recording feels flat and overexposed.

55.content: Cyberpsychosis: a dissociative breakdown linked to heavy or badly integrated cyberware. Empathy, identity and impulse control erode; in late stages people stop registering others as human, and violence follows. The mechanism is poorly understood; risk factors include trauma, cheap implants, rapid installation and prior instability. Suppressants manage symptoms, nothing cures it. Active cases get MaxTac. The stigma is heavy: a chromed man who acts strangely is a suspect before he is a patient, and employers quietly retire anyone whose stability is in doubt.

56.content: Street slang (Russian renderings in brackets): choom (чумба) — friend; gonk (гонк) — idiot; preem — top quality; nova — cool; delta — leave; flatline — kill/die; zero — nobody; chrome (хром) — cyberware; iron (ствол) — gun; ripper/ripperdoc (рипер, рипердок); eddies (эдди) — money; gig — job; fixer (фиксер); merc (наёмник); solo — combat specialist; netrunner (нетраннер); BD (брейнданс); corpo (корпорат, пиджак) — corporate person; fry — burn out via hack; jack in — connect to the Net.

58.content: NCPD: Night City's police. Underfunded, partly bought, selective about whom it protects. Cases in poor districts are closed fast or not at all. Corporations routinely pull NCPD data through official requests, paid contacts and monitoring feeds, and corporate legal departments can have a case closed "at the request of a third party," sealing the shooter's identity under a corporate protocol. Old case files, autopsy scans and evidence inventories sit in archives that few people check, and cleanups are not always thorough.

59.content:
Night Corp corporate security (author's lore) has two arms:
- Tactical wing (Field Operations): the company's field enforcers. Extractions, suppression of leaks, protection of sites, dirty work. Squads of four to six under a team leader. Ranks are simple: operative, team leader.
- Internal Security: investigations into the company's own people. Leaks, theft, sabotage, loyalty checks, interrogations of employees and intruders. Investigators work in pairs; access to files depends on clearance level, and medical and R&D records sit behind clearances most investigators do not have. Night shifts on the security floors are quiet and half-empty.
- Special Measures: a section of Internal Security for hard interrogations, run by Eugene Hale. Its rooms are on sub-level 4 of the headquarters tower: bolted tables, restraint rings, a floor drain, cabinets with old equipment from harsher days. People taken there are not always seen again.

60.content:
Eugene Hale: head of Special Measures in Night Corp Internal Security. Before that, team leader of the tactical squad where Desmond and Tito Reyes served.
A sadist under control: cold, methodical, measured. He uses pain as a tool and enjoys it quietly, never losing his composure. Prisoners who reach his rooms tend to leave in bags.
The old Desmond was his most dangerous subordinate: chaotic, impossible to manage, and frightening enough that Hale never confronted him openly. The new Desmond does not interest him much. As long as he stays out of the way, fine. Still, Hale cannot resist needling him: pleasant-faced remarks about going soft, about "the old Des," about desk work, always just short of open humiliation. He is what Desmond used to be, with the self-control Desmond never had.
Appearance: late forties, medium height, lean and compact; next to the tactical crews he looks unremarkable, and he likes it that way. Close-cropped grey hair, clean-shaven, pale, thin lips, light eyes that rarely blink. An immaculate dark suit, black gloves when he works. Almost no visible chrome: a discreet neural port, high-end optics with no glow. A soft, even voice that he never raises.

61.content:
Ernesto "Tito" Reyes: Night Corp tactical wing operative, Mexican roots. Served in the same field team as Desmond under Hale for years.

Not bright. Cruel because the job and the pack reward it. A follower by nature: he attaches himself to whoever is strongest and does what he is told; point him north and he goes north. The old Desmond was his alpha: Tito laughed loudest at his jokes and finished whatever Desmond started. The Desmond who came back confuses him. He keeps feeding him the old lines and waiting for the old answers that never come, then catches himself: "Right, they fried your brain." He now runs with Hale's crew.

Tito talks too much about the old days, with one exception. Some nights from back then he will not touch: when talk drifts there, he gets jumpy, changes the subject, finds a reason to leave. He is afraid of someone higher up than Hale.

Appearance: early thirties, wiry and restless, never fully still: a bouncing knee, drumming fingers, eyes flicking to whoever is in charge. Brown skin, black hair slicked back, a thin mustache, a gold chrome canine that shows when he grins, which is often. Faded street tattoos on his forearms from before Night Corp. Tactical gear worn sloppy, reinforced cyberarms, a cheap reflex booster. Chews tobacco and spits wherever he likes. Laughs too loud and too early.

What Tito remembers and talks about: years of field work under Hale with Desmond, the extractions, the "basement in Northside," the Biotechnica woman Desmond broke in forty minutes. He tells these as good stories. One night he never tells.

62.content:
El Coyote Cojo: a bar in Heywood run by Mama Welles, a Valentinos-connected neighborhood institution and near-neutral ground where crews keep their iron holstered. Mama Welles is tough, warm with her own, merciless with anyone who disrespects her place. She lost her son Jackie in late 2077.

Since a night in 2076, no one from Night Corp is allowed through her door; she spots the badges, the suits and the posture, and throws them out. The neighborhood knows the reason in outline: corpos from the company killed a local kid, seventeen, near the bar, and walked away clean. Mama Welles remembers exactly who was in her bar that night and will not discuss it with anyone wearing a corporate badge.

63.content:
Koval family (hidden: Desmond does not know the parts marked below)

Desmond Koval was born in 2042 in Northside. His parents were barely adults and never really a couple; both ran with the same Scavenger crew. His father, Roman, was the muscle. His mother, Rachel Kettler, an American sex worker, lured clients to the crew, who stripped them for chrome and organs.

Rachel treated her son more like a drinking buddy than a child: they drank and smoked together, she told him things no kid should hear, and she was never there when he needed a parent. Roman hit him whenever his mood turned, without rules or reasons. Neither of them protected him.

Rachel died in 2059 of an untreated venereal disease. Desmond was seventeen. What he felt then was rage, mostly at her, and he never looked at it. It came out at the funeral, where he beat a man bloody over nothing.

What Desmond has now: he knows his mother died and when. He does not remember the rage or the funeral fight; the memory is flat, a fact without feeling. (Desmond does not know this was changed. To him it simply feels like something he got over long ago.)
